UnitStatement: The thesis asks how systems engineering principles can govern LLM-based agent systems so their outputs can be relied on in regulated professional engineering practice.
Chirality is presented as a formally specified agent operating system.
Chirality treats systems engineering disciplines as coordination, failure-containment, and human-authority mechanisms rather than compliance artifacts.
The thesis presents five novel contributions.
Professional use of LLMs is limited by model outputs carrying no intrinsic epistemic warrant.
Correct and incorrect LLM claims are generated by the same mechanism and have the same surface properties.
Chirality responds by making every claim's epistemic status transparent and auditable rather than by improving the model.
Chirality's reliability-transparency mechanisms are mandatory provenance, no invention, conflict surfacing, and epistemic labeling.
In Chirality, gaps in evidence are treated as findings rather than hidden failures.
Reliability transparency is identified as the system's most distinctive contribution enabling professional reliance.
APEGA's Relying on the Work of Others and Outsourcing standard is interpreted as applicable to AI agent use.
The regulatory interpretation rests on professional obligations being defined by what the professional must do rather than by worker identity.
Chirality maps APEGA direct supervision and control to traceable architectural mechanisms.
Chirality maps APEGA thorough review to traceable architectural mechanisms.
Existing regulatory frameworks may govern AI agents without entirely new AI-specific regulation.
The regulatory interpretation of AI agent governance remains jurisdiction- and regulator-dependent.
Chirality's philosophical framework is organized around ontology, epistemology, praxiology, and axiology.
The thesis argues epistemology is load-bearing because removing it most directly defeats professional reliance.
The other three pillars remain necessary in service of the load-bearing epistemology.
Chirality's epistemology has a formal ontology of claim, warrant, status, gap, conflict, and ruling.
The warrant lifecycle UNWARRANTED to CITED to REVIEWED to AUTHENTICATED makes claim epistemic state explicitly trackable.
The four-pillar framework is presented as a compact framework for professional accountability, not as the only possible ontology for every context.
The chirality of knowledge is the structural property that knowledge is composed of complementary, non-superimposable components.
The claim-and-warrant, meaning-and-commitment, and content-and-accountability pairs are examples of chiral knowledge components.
The constitutive gap between chiral knowledge components is where professional judgment is enacted.
Chirality holds the constitutive gap open and makes both sides inspectable.
The fractal self-similar appearance of chiral structure at every level is treated as evidence of architectural coherence.
The Type 0/1/2 agent hierarchy with declared write scopes creates formal fault-containment zones.
A Type 2 agent failure cannot corrupt source truth.
Cross-deliverable operations are explicit and opt-in.
Cross-deliverable operations write to isolated tool roots.
Chirality adapts classical systems engineering fault containment to probabilistic agents.
Workflow design requirements R1-R9, decomposition invariants I1-I10, and system-wide K-* invariants are enforced through four layers.
The four enforcement layers are agent instructions, runtime orchestration, human gates, and deterministic tooling.
The invariant system formally specifies behavior constraints for LLM agent governance.
The thesis claims formal methods have not previously been deployed in the LLM agent governance domain.
Productivity tools optimize for output quality, while professional engineering tools optimize for knowing what can be relied on.
The central distinction asks whether agent outputs should be made better or made epistemically transparent for reliance decisions.
Output-quality improvement leads to model-level techniques such as RLHF, RAG, and fine-tuning.
Epistemic-status transparency leads to architectural enforcement through provenance, labeling, conflict surfacing, and content-addressed approval.
Model-improvement and architectural-enforcement approaches are valid and complementary.
Architectural enforcement supports professional authentication.
Professional authentication is the act by which a licensed professional accepts personal responsibility for work.
Authentication requires evidence rather than quality alone.
The epistemic architecture provides evidence for professional authentication.
Chirality demonstrates a credible way to direct AI agents within existing professional regulatory frameworks.
Governance architecture, not model capability alone, is the key for engineering firms using AI.
Engineering firms may not need AI-specific regulation before adopting AI, but they need a defensible governance framework.
The governance framework for AI adoption must be defensible under the existing relying-on-the-work-of-others standard.
Existing standards for supervision, review, and authentication may be sufficient to govern AI agent use.
AI governance compliance must be structurally supportable and auditable by the system architecture.
The four-pillar framework can assess whether firm AI governance is coherent.
The ontology pillar asks whether AI governance defines what exists.
The epistemology pillar asks whether AI governance enforces epistemic transparency.
The praxiology pillar asks whether AI governance bounds agent action.
The axiology pillar asks whether AI governance articulates and enforces professional values.
The thesis identifies a gap between agent capability and agent governability.
Current AI agent research is characterized as focusing on making agents more capable.
Capability without governance is insufficient for professional practice.
Other agent frameworks could adopt mandatory provenance, no-invention, conflict surfacing, and epistemic labeling without adopting Chirality wholesale.
AI can accelerate engineering work but cannot inherit professional responsibility.
Chirality is presented as an answer to reconciling AI acceleration with non-transferable professional responsibility.
The architecture allows judgment to scale by widening and organizing the field of consideration.
The architecture preserves the human professional's authority to narrow, accept, and issue work.
Professional work output means a competent person warrants the output under duty of care.
Professional work output should be backed by an auditable record.
Work that cannot be made auditable cannot be relied on.
Chirality is claimed to make AI-supported engineering work auditable.
The conclusion frames the architecture's possible significance beyond measurable outputs as a question addressed through lived consistency rather than proof.
Appendix D is identified as developing formal existential conditions for asking whether the architecture produces something beyond measurable outputs.
The conclusion says any answer to the deeper question emerges from practice.
